speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is strong—is strong overall and has made significant progress toward our goals over the past two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Labor market conditions have cooled from their formerly overheated state and remain solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has moved much closer to our 2 percent longer-run goal, though it remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged and to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has continued to expand at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For 2024 as a whole, GDP looks to have risen above 2 percent, bolstered by resilient consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Investment in equipment and intangibles appears to have slowed in the fourth quarter but was strong for the year overall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Following weakness in the middle of last year, activity in the housing sector seems to have stabilized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions remain solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 170,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Following earlier increases, the unemployment rate has stabilized since the middle of last year and, at 4.1 percent in December, remains low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has eased over the past year, and the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a wide set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are broadly in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is not a source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly over the past two years but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.6 percent over the 12 months ending in December and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecasters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals as being roughly in balance, and we are attentive to the risks on both sides of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the course of our three previous meetings, we lowered our policy rate by a full percentage point from its peak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That recalibration of our policy stance was appropriate in light of the progress on inflation and the rebalancing in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With our policy stance significantly less restrictive than it had been and the economy remaining strong, we do not need to be in a hurry to adjust our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4¼ to 4½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy restraint too fast or too much could hinder progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing policy restraint too slowly or too little could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering the extent and timing of additional adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not on any preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the economy evolves, we will adjust our policy stance in a manner that best promotes our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy remains—economy remains strong and inflation does not continue to move sustainably toward 2 percent, we can maintain policy restraint for longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, we can ease policy accordingly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we previously announced, our five-year review, review of our monetary policy framework is taking place this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At this meeting, the Committee began its discussions by reviewing the context and outcomes of our previous review that concluded in 2020 as well as the experiences of other central banks in conducting reviews.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our review will again include outreach and public events involving a wide range of parties, including Fed Listens events around the country and a research conference in May.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Throughout this process, we will be open to new ideas and critical feedback, and we will take on board lessons of the last five years in determining our findings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We intend to wrap up the review by late summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would note that the Committee’s 2 percent longer-run inflation goal will, will be retained and will not be a focus of the review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy: maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-run inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Mr. Chairman, Steve Liesman from CNBC.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Mr. Chairman, all right, at an event in Davos—or from, to Davos, anyway—the President said he’ll demand that interest rates drop immediately.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: So I guess I have a three-part question.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Has the President done this to you?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Has he made that demand?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Secondly, what is your response to that?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And, third, what effect, if anything—if any, does a President making these kind of remarks have on policy?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Three questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m seeing, seeing it really as one question, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, I, I’m not going to have—I’m not going to have any, any response or comment whatsoever on, on what the President’s said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not appropriate for me to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The public should be confident that we will continue to do our work as we always have—focusing on using our tools to achieve our goals, and really keeping our heads down and doing our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s how we best serve the public.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Could you just comment on whether he’s physically communicated his demand to you?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve had no contact.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos, the Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chair Powell, you and several of your colleagues said around the time of the last meeting that your policy stance was “meaningfully restrictive.” Given economic and financial market developments since then, how has your confidence changed in an assessment that says interest rates are meaningfully restrictive?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think that my assessment really has changed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, a couple of things have happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve gotten more strong data, but we’ve also seen rates move up at the long end, which could represent a tightening in financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think if we look back over the past year or so, we can see that policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at the effect of high rates on interest-sensitive spending—for example, in housing—and if you look at the achievement of our goal variables, we’re seeing the economy move toward 2 percent inflation and, and has moved largely to maximum employment, so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Though we literally look at the—at the—at movement toward the goal variables to make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, policy is meaningfully less restrictive than it was before we began to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s 100 basis points less restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And for that reason, you know, we’re going to be focusing on seeing real progress on inflation or, alternatively, some weakness in the labor market before we—before we consider making adjustments.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: If I could follow up.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Does the economy here warrant meaningfully restrictive interest rates, and would you judge interest rates to still be meaningfully restrictive if you were to lower them by another ¼ point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, I, I think our policy stance is very well calibrated, as I mentioned, to balance the achievement of our two—of our two goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we want to—policy to be restrictive enough to continue to foster further, further progress for our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, we don’t need to see further weakening in the labor market to achieve that goal, and that’s kind of what we’ve been getting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market has really been broadly stable; the unemployment rate has been broadly stable now for six months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Conditions seem to be broadly in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say, look at the last couple of inflation readings and you see we don’t—we don’t overreact to two good readings or two bad readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, nonetheless, the last couple of readings have suggested, you know, more positive readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I think we’re—I think policy’s well, well positioned.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Colby, from the New York Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Colby Smith, with the New York Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Chair Powell, how should we interpret the removal of the line from the statement that inflation has made progress towards the 2 percent goal?

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Is that no longer the case?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, so let me look—if you just look at the first paragraph, we did a little bit of language cleanup there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We took out a reference to “since earlier in the year” as it related to the labor market, and we just chose to, to shorten that sentence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, I, I mean, if you look at the sort of intermeeting data was good, and, and there was—there was another inflation reading, I guess, just before the December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, we’ve got two, two good readings in a row that are consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, we’re not going to overinterpret two good or two bad readings, but this was not meant to send a signal other than this: You know, you, you can take away from all of this that we remain committed to achieving our 2 percent inflation goal sustainably.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And just to follow up: We’ve seen inflation expectations across a number of measures rise sharply—which has, in part, been linked to tariff concerns.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: But there’s also been this encouraging data that you mentioned in terms of CPI and rent indices.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: So how would you characterize concerns about upside risks to inflation across the Committee, especially those tied to policies related to the Trump Administration?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well I, I’d say you, you see expectations moving up a little bit, at the short end—but not at the longer run, which [is] where it really matters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And those could be related to—could be related to what you mentioned, some of the new policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think where the Committee is very much in the mode of waiting to see what policies are enacted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, and we, we don’t know what will happen with, with tariffs, with immigration, with fiscal policy, and with regulatory policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re only just beginning to see—actually, are not really beginning to see much, and I think we need to—we need to let those policies be articulated before we can even begin to make a, a plausible assessment of what their implications for the economy will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re going to be watching carefully and, and, as we always do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is no different than any other set of policy changes at the beginning of a—of an Administration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll patiently watch and understand and, and, you know, kind of not be in a hurry to, to get to a place of understanding what our policy response should be until we see how it plays out.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Michael McKee.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Michael McKee from Bloomberg Television and Radio.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: You and your colleagues normally condition future policy moves with the phrase, “if the economy develops as we anticipate.” Is it fair to say that since there’s a lot unknown about what this Administration’s fiscal policies are actually going to be that you don’t have a medium- to long-term economic forecast that you can have confidence in?

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Or, if that’s not true, can you lay out what you think is going to happen in the economy, how you see it developing?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, at all times—at all times, forecasts are conditional, at a minimum, on just a set of expectations, and, and they’re highly uncertain in both directions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we know that economic forecasting is, is really difficult, beyond just a month or two out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So in the current situation, there’s probably some elevated uncertainty because of, of, you know, significant policy shifts in those four areas that I mentioned: tariffs, tariffs, immigration, fiscal policy, and, and regulatory policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s probably some additional uncertainty, but that should be passing; we should go through that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then we’ll be back to the regular amount of uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, what, what forecasters are doing—not just us, but everybody’s doing—is they’ve got sort of just a set of assumptions about what might happen, but they’re really kind of in the nature of a placeholder, and—meaning, you know, plausible, could be, but honestly you wouldn’t stand behind it because you just don’t know, and so you’re just—you’re just on hold, waiting to see what comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s, it’s a very large economy, and policies affect it at the margin, but we’ll, you know, we’re going to wait and see.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: If I could follow up.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: The idea that you feel the—that policy is restrictive suggests that the Fed, in general, wants to continue to lower interest rates.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: So when you look at the data that you are dependent on, are you looking for data that tell you that you can cut or data that will tell you [that] you should hold?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re—we’re looking—it’s more the other—the way—the way it works is, we are looking at the data to guide us in what we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, that, that’s what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And right now, we feel like we’re in a very good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy’s well positioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy’s in, in quite a good place, actually, as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what, what we do expect is to see further progress on inflation, and, you know, as I mentioned, as we see that—or if we were to see weakening in the labor market that could foster—we could then be in a position of, of making further adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, right now, we, we don’t see that, and we see things as in a really good place for policy and for the economy, and so we feel like we don’t need to be in a hurry to, to make any adjustments.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Howard.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Howard Schneider with Reuters.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thank you very much.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: In 2021, at a central bank conference, you said, quote, “Throughout my career in both public and private sectors, I’ve seen that the best and most successful organizations are often the ones that have a strong and persistent commitment to diversity and inclusion.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: These organizations consistently attract the best talent by investing in and retaining a world-class workforce.” Question, first question is, do you still believe that?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: And if so, how do you intend to put that belief into practice while remaining consistent with the recent executive order prohibiting diversity and inclusion efforts?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me say, “yes,” in answer to your first question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, to the second question, I want to say this: We are, like others, we’re reviewing the orders and the associated details as they are made available.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as has been our practice over many Administrations, we are working to align our policies with the executive orders as appropriate and consistent with applicable law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I want to add that I’m not going to have anything more specific for you today on this whole set of issues.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Well, if I could just follow up quickly on that.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: I’m wondering how you’re getting that to be consistent with the Dodd-Frank law’s stipulations about maintaining an Office of Minority and Women Inclusion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I did—I did mention “consistent with applicable law,” right?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Which is governing.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Elizabeth.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Thanks so much.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Elizabeth Schulze with ABC News.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Just to follow up on Steve’s question, what reassurance can you give the American public that the Fed will continue to operate independent of politics under this Administration?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I’ve—as I’ve said countless times over the years, this is—this is who we are; this is what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We study the data, we, we analyze how it will affect the outlook and the balance of risks, and we use our tools to try to give it our best understanding, our best thinking, try to achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we do; that’s always what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t look for us to do anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—you know, lots of research shows that’s the—that’s the best way for a central bank to operate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’ll give us the best possible chance to achieve these goals for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s always what we’re going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And people should have confidence in that, as I—as I said a few minutes ago.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: You’ve said that the Fed is in wait-and-see mode, based on the policies that come out of this Administration.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Has the Fed started to model what policies like mass deportations, changes in immigration policy, specifically, would look like for the workforce and for inflation?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So one of the things our, our staff does is they, they look at a range of possible outcomes, and, and they, they tend to go from really good to really bad, and, you know, it’s, it’s one of the best things that they do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And in each Tealbook—you can look at the five-year-old Tealbooks and see their alternative simulations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what they do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They, it’ll be a baseline, and then they’ll show six or seven alternative scenarios, including really good ones and, and not-so-good ones.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what those do is they spark, you know, the, the policymakers to sort of think and understand about the, you know, the, the uncertainties that surround this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yes, we, we—staff does that, and we, we’re all well aware that there are—that the range of possibilities is always broad, and—not just now, but always.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you have to—it’s hard to be open to just how, how broad the possibilities are for an economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, no one saw the pandemic coming, and it was—you know, it changed everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So things happen, and—but yes, we do—we do do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s, it’s one thing to do that to make assessments about what might happen and begin to think about what you might do in that case, but you don’t act until you—until you see much more than we see now.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Catarina.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: Catarina Saraiva, Bloomberg News.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: You know, last month you talked about a future rate cut as being pretty, you know, significantly predicated on more progress in inflation.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: With the characterization of the labor market in the statement today, would you say that that’s even more so the case now?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’d say it’s the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we, we want to see, you know, further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, the story’s there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, it’s—we’re just going to have to see the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the end of the day, it, it comes down to 12-month inflation, because that takes out the seasonality issues that may exist.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’re, we’re just going to need to see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think that—we think we see the pathway for that to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One, one example—a key example—is that you now do see owner’s equivalent rent and, you know, housing services—the way it’s calculated for PCE [prices], you see that coming down pretty steadily now, and that’s the—that’s the place where the, most of the remaining gap is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, a big part of the overrun, as you will know, was [coming] from nonmarket services [prices], which don’t tend to send much signal [about future inflation].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you can look through all that and, and think, “Okay, that then we seem to be set up for further progress.” But being seem to set up for it is one thing; having it is another.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we’re going to want to see further, further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Remember, we’re not, you know, we’re, we’re under—2 percent, but our goal is 2 percent, and we do mean to get back sustainably to 2 percent.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: And, and in terms of the labor market, I mean, how—is that broadly—you know, you said a broad set of indicators show that it’s in pretty solid place.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: Was there broad agreement on that?

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: There’s been a few underlying indicators that are showing perhaps some weakness: a low hiring rate, you know, workers reporting that it’s increasingly difficult to find a job.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: Is that of concern to the Committee?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, we look at, of course, a very broad range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, so, it starts with unemployment—sorry, with, yeah, with the unemployment rate, employment participation, wages, job quits—are people quitting?—that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The ratio of vacancies to unemployed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at all those things, and you, you put your finger, though, on—it’s a low—it’s a low-hiring environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you have a job, it’s all—it’s all good, but if you—if you have to find a job, the job-finding rate—the hiring rates have come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, that’s more typical of a—let’s say—let’s say that the unemployment—that the—that the labor market is at a sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not overheated anymore.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think we need it to cool off anymore.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do watch it extremely carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s one of our two goal variables.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, yeah, I, I’d say we watch those things quite carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But nonetheless, overall, look at the aggregate data in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It does seem to—the labor market does seem, seem to be pretty stable and broadly in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When you’ve got a, an unemployment rate that is—that has been pretty stable now for, for a, a full half a year.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence with Fox Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: On employment, now, you said there’s a broad range of possibilities, but last September you said, quote, “We understand that there’s been quite an influx across the borders, and that has actually been one of things that’s allowed unemployment rate to rise.” Now that the flow over the border has slowed and we’re seeing deportations, how do you expect the unemployment rate to react?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, so what’s happening is that the, the flows across the border have decreased very significantly, and there’s every reason to expect that to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so—but job creation has come down a bit, too, so, you know, if those two things come down together, that, that sort of can be a reason for the unemployment rate to stabilize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In other words, a breakeven rate—as, as population growth slows, the breakeven rate that you need in new jobs to make—to, to make jobs for, for workers declines as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that seems to be something about what’s happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You, you do see a very—a very flat unemployment rate at a time when you’ve seen significant declines [in job growth].

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: I want to ask you about Fed employment.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: I know that tax money is not used here, but Elon Musk alleges that the Fed is, quote, “absurdly overstaffed.” We’ve seen the Executive Branch push to reduce the federal workforce.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: I just want to get your reaction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we, we run a very careful budget process where we’re fully aware that what, that, you know, we owe the—we owe that to the public, and we believe we do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I’ve got no further comment than that, thanks.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Chris.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Chris Rugaber at Associated Press.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: President Trump has said he will lower inflation by reducing gas and energy costs.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Do you see such costs as a particular driver of inflation, and would lowering them have a dramatic effect?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Chris, I’m not going to—I’m not going to react or discuss anything that, that any elected politician might say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’ll give you a mulligan.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Okay, oh, thank you.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Well, nearly two weeks ago the Fed said it was withdrawing from the Network for Greening the Financial System even as, you know, even as we have significant wildfires in Los Angeles doing billions of dollars in damage.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: And, of course, the NGFS, as you know, is a group to talk about how the financial system could address climate change.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Many commentators did see the timing as political.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Why did you leave that organization?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Can you explain that decision?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure, I’d be glad to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we considered this, you know, really at length, and we did decide to withdraw from the NGFS.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, really, the reason is that the, the work that the NGFS does has broadened very significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Think about nature-related risks and biodiversity and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, the, the work of the NGFS is, is, in, in significant part intended to—and this is a quote—“mobilize mainstream finance to support the transition toward a sustainable economy.” So we joined to get the benefit of understanding what other central banks were doing and, and seeing research and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think this is just way beyond any plausible mandate that you could attribute to the Fed, and so we have a quite narrow role, as I’ve—as I’ve said many times, and I think that, that the activities of the NGFS are not a good fit for the Fed, given our current mandate and authority.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, and I just think it was time to acknowledge that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the, the process—this process dates back—thinking about it dates back a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I made the decision to bring this to the Board, you know, some months ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just—it just—the process just took time to get here, and, and this is when—this is when we, we got in and voted on it, so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’m aware of how it can look, but it was really not driven by politics; it was driven by kind of the disconnect between the work of the NGFS and our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Other central banks have different mandates and belong to the NGFS.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have no, no criticism of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it just isn’t—it’s not right for the Fed.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Andrew.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Andrew Ackerman with the Washington Post.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: I’m wondering if you could talk more about what further progress would look like for consumers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, 2 percent—inflation down to—inflation down to 2 percent sustainably is what, what we’re trying to achieve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re, we’re somewhat above that, as you know, and, you know, we, we want to see, you know, serial readings that suggest that we’re making further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And consumers will, will pick that up, of course, in the things that they buy at the grocery store or at the store.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: The other thing I wanted to ask was just how far away you think you are from neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, you can’t know with any precision, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I like to say, that you know that—you know the neutral rate by its works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, you know, at 4.3 percent we’re, we’re above pretty much everyone on the Committee’s estimates of the longer-run neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think our eyes are telling us that our policy is having the effects on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s really the question we ask.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you can consult models, empirical models, theoretical models.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You really have to just look out the window and see how your—how your policy rate is affecting the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think we see that it’s having meaningful effects in bringing inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has helped bring the labor market into balance as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I would say we’re meaningfully above it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I am—I, I have no illusion that, that anyone knows precisely how much that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, but it, you know—not knowing that, and having cut 100 basis points, means that it’s appropriate that we—that we not be in a hurry to make further adjustments.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Victoria.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Victoria Guida with Politico.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: So, as a general matter, when it comes to executive orders and OMB memos, do those always apply to the Fed, sometimes, never, or do you just often voluntarily comply?

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: What is—what is the legality there?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s been—it’s been our practice, as I mentioned, to work to align our policies to those that are mentioned in, in the executive orders.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—I’m just going to leave it at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, I’m not going to—I’m not going to go any deeper than that or, or get into any deeper into this set of issues today.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Claire.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Claire Jones from the Financial Times.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Two questions, if I may, on tariffs.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Well, first of all, we’ve seen global trade wars before, notably in 2019 last time around.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: But then we were then in a very different place on both inflation and growth.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: If we see tariffs of the same sort of magnitude that we got then—which I know is a big if—what do you think might be different this time around?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: And, secondly, Tiff Macklem said there was no doubt that the threat of tariffs was a big driver of the cut by the Bank of Canada today.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: What sort of information would the Fed need to see on tariffs before it was willing to take such a preemptive move?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sorry, make a—?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: To—what sort of information would you need to see on tariffs?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Would you need to see a strategy, actual implementation, actual movement of inflation expectations, before you’re actually willing to change the path of monetary policy on the basis of it?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we just—so first of all, thing, things are a little different now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve just come through a high-inflation period, and you can argue that both ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can— you can say that companies have figured out that they do like to raise prices, but, but we also hear a lot from companies these days that consumers have really had it with price increases, and so I don’t know how that shakes out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, you’re coming through a situation where we’re not quite back to 2 percent, and that, that’s just different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, you know, the trade—the kind of footprint of trade is, has changed a, a lot, as trade is now spread around the, you know—it’s not as concentrated in China as it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There was a lot more manufacturing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It moved to Mexico and other places.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so there were differences, and I just think the, the range of possibilities is, is very, very wide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just don’t know, and I, I don’t want to start speculating, as tempting as it is, because we really don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we didn’t know, by the way, in, I guess, 2018.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, we didn’t really know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it, you know, the—again, the range of possibilities, very, very wide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know what’s going to be tariff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know for how long or how much, what countries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know about retaliation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know how it’s going to transmit through the economy to consumers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that really does remain to be seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, there are lots of places where that—where that—where that price increase from the tariff can show up between the manufacturer and a consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Just so many variables.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re just going to have to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, the best we can do is what we’ve done, which is study up on this and, you know, look at historical experience, read the literature, and think about the factors that might matter, and then we’ll just have to see—have to see how it—how it goes.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Courtenay.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Courtenay Brown from Axios.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Two unrelated questions.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: The first is whether or not there was any discussion about QT and the timeline for ending QT at this meeting.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: And then the second question is just—I wonder if the AI-prompted selloff in the stock market this week signaled anything to you about the state of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, on QT, on—let’s, let’s talk about runoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the most recent data do suggest that reserves are still abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Reserves remain roughly as high as they were when runoff began.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the federal funds rate has been very steady within the target range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We track a, a bunch of metrics, and they do tend to point to, to reserves being abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do intend to reduce the size of our balance sheet to a level that’s consistent with implementing monetary policy efficiently and effectively in our ample-reserves regime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re closely monitoring a, a range of indicators to assess conditions, and that should provide signals whether reserves are approaching a level that could be judged as, quote, “somewhat above ample.” I, I don’t have anything to say to you about particular dates; it’s just that’s the process, and what we see is, is that, that rates do appear to be abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As always, we stand ready to take appropriate action to support the smooth transition of monetary policy, including to adjust the details of our approach for reducing the size of the balance sheet in light of economic and financial developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On, on AI, it’s a big event in, in the stock market and in particular parts of the stock market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, what, what really matters for us is macro developments, and that means substantial changes in financial conditions that are persistent for a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t put that label on, on these events, although of course we’re all watching it with interest.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Simon.

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: Simon Rabinovitch with the Economist, thank you.

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: You mentioned in your remarks that activity in the housing sector seems to have stabilized.

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: At the same time, since your first rate cut in September, long-term mortgage rates have gone up by a full percentage point, back above 7 percent.

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: I’m wondering, kind of looking forward, do you think—are you confident that activity will remain stable, given how elevated mortgage rates are?

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: How does it fit into your broader thinking about the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, as you know, as we’ve reduced our, our policy rate 100 basis points, longer rates have gone up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not because of expectations—not principally because of expectations about our policy or about inflation; it’s more a term premium story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, and, you know, it’s long rates that matter for, for housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I don’t think—I think these higher rates are going to—they’re, they’re probably hold back housing activities to some extent, if they’re persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll have to see how long they persist.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we, we are—we control an overnight rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Generally, it, it propagates through the whole family of asset prices, including interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in this particular case, it’s all happened at a time when, for reasons unrelated to our policy, longer rates have moved up.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jennifer.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Jennifer Schonberger with Yahoo Finance.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: You said you want to see further progress on inflation.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Given that households appear to be unhappy with the elevated level of prices, do you believe the Committee should wait until inflation has fallen back to target to cut rates again?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, I wouldn’t say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we’ve never said we need to be all the way at target to reduce rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At, at any time, what we’re doing is we’re looking at the economy and asking whether our policy stance is the right one to achieve maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I think if—we would want to see further progress, but we think our—we think our—as I mentioned, we think that our policy stance is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Meaningfully restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not highly restrictive, but meaningfully restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I would think we need to see further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say all the way back down to 2 percent on a sustainable basis, although we’d love to see that, of course, and we will.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: And a separate question for you, on tariffs.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Curious whether the threat of tariffs and not knowing whether they could stick or not creates uncertainty for business here in the United States and could cause them to pull back, ultimately weighing on growth.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Does the threat of tariffs cause you to ponder your growth forecast?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we—I want to avoid commenting, even indirectly, on the conduct of tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s not our job, and it’s not our job to comment on the moves that people make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I wouldn’t want to criticize anything that’s happening or really comment on it one way or another—praise it, for that matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just not our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I do think that—you know, we found in, in 2018, [when] there was a lot of work done on trade policy uncertainty, trade policy uncertainty, if it’s large and persistent, can start to matter for businesses making investment decisions and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not something I’m observing today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very early days for this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that did—I think that did matter in 2018–19.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and it’s one, you know, one of many things we’ll be watching.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Matt Egan.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Matt Egan from CNN.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Following up on Courtenay’s question from earlier about the stock market, how concerned are you, if at all, about potential asset bubble brewing in financial markets?

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: How do relatively high market valuations factor into considerations about potentially lowering interest rates further?

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Is that something that’s in the back of your mind?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we look—we look at, from a financial stability perspective, at asset prices generally, along with things like leverage in the household sector, leverage in the banking system, funding risk for banks, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s just one of the four things, asset prices are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, yeah, I, I’d say they’re elevated by, by many metrics right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good part of that, of course, is this thing around tech and AI, but we, we look at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we also—we look at how resilient the households and, and businesses and the financial sector are to those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at that mainly from our financial stability perspective, and we think that there’s a lot of resilience out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Banks have high capital, and households are actually, overall—not all households, but in, in the aggregate, households are in pretty good shape financially these days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how we think about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, you know, we, we also—we look at overall financial conditions, and you’ve got—you can’t just take—you can’t just take equity prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got to look at rates, too, and that, you know, that represents a, a tightening in conditions, with higher rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, financial conditions are probably still somewhat accommodative, but it’s a mixed bag.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Richard.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: I’m Richard Escobedo with CBS News.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: One question for you.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: This month’s statement notes that unemployment has stabilized at a low rate and that the labor market is solid.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: You walked through some of what’s driving this, but I wonder what risks you see that might challenge your assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, the things we watch, we discussed earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One, one is, is that there’s a low hiring rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that if, if there were to be a spike in layoffs, if companies were to start to reduce headcount, you would see unemployment go up pretty quickly, because the hiring rate is quite low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that’s one thing we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s also—it’s worth pointing out that for lower-income households, they are—they’re under significant pressure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And in the aggregate, the numbers are good, but we know that people at the lower end of the income spectrum are, are struggling with, with costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, really, it’s, it’s high inflation for the basics of life.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not so much the inflation now; it’s the price level, because inflation has raised prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is now closer—much closer to target, but people are really feeling that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, overall, this is a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Here you’re at 4.1 percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s just a really good level, and you’ve been solidly there now for six, seven months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And job creation is pretty close to a level that will hold the unemployment rate there, given, given that, you know, there’ll be much slower population growth.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: One more question.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: Some of the uncertainty around immigration policy.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: Is—in your assessment, is that making it harder for businesses and the Fed to plan going forward?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we hear anecdotal reports, but I, I don’t see—there’s nothing in the data yet on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you do—you hear—you hear that kind of thing about construction, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you know, businesses that are dependent on immigrant labor are, are saying that it’s, it’s suddenly gotten harder to, to get people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I, again—I know—you don’t see that in the aggregate data yet, but yes, you, you hear it anecdotally.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICHOLAS JASINSKI
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: NICHOLAS JASINSKI
sentence: Nicholas Jasinski from Barron’s.

speaker: NICHOLAS JASINSKI
sentence: The uncertainty is certainly a theme today, and I’m wondering, are there any periods from your career, or as it relates to markets, the economy, what’s going on here in Washington and beyond, or from lessons from history, that may provide some guidance for a central banker operating in uncertain times like today?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I guess I’d say this: Uncertainty is, is with us all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, it is human nature, apparently, to underestimate the—how fat the tails are, in a way, that, you know, the, the possibility—we think of things in a normal distribution, and in the economy it’s not a normal distribution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The tails are very fat, meaning things can happen way out of your expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s never not that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t—you know, if you—if you think about it—think about the first few months of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That was uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Are we going to be able to reopen the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If so, when?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: How much of it?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: How long will it take?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, that was uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we have now is a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have the economy growing at, you know, 2 to 2½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation’s come down to, to now the, you know—the headline inflation number was 2.6 [percent], and that’s what the public experiences.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at—we look at core because it’s a better indicator of future inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yes, the price level went up a lot for inflation, and people are feeling that, and, and they’re not wrong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I—so the kind of uncertainty we have is just a, a usual level of uncertainty about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But then policies—which are, you know, not for us to criticize or, or praise, really—those are—those are policies which people are, have been elected to implement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re implementing them with a view to, to making a better economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I, I don’t think—I wouldn’t call this out as, as a—as one of those times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t compare it to the Global Financial Crisis or anything like that, given that we have actually a very good economy right now.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Evan.

speaker: EVAN RYSER
sentence: Evan Ryser with Market News International.

speaker: EVAN RYSER
sentence: Chair Powell, is a March cut still on the table?

speaker: EVAN RYSER
sentence: And then, additionally, are you looking to see better-than-expected data on inflation to cut, or are you looking for inflation data that roughly aligns with current forecasts?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, as, as I mentioned, the economy’s strong, the labor market’s solid, downside risks to the labor market appear to have abated, and we think disinflation continues on a slow and sometimes bumpy path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That tells me and the other members of the Committee—the broad sense of the Committee, actually, is that we don’t need to be in a hurry to adjust our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Your second question was?

speaker: EVAN RYSER
sentence: Whether or not you need to see better-than-expected inflation data or just inflation data that roughly aligns with your current forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s one of those things we’ll know it when we see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But more, more the—the expectation is that we will make continued progress, and, you know, that’s what we want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we’ll know it when we see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When we—it, it’s going to have to be something that isn’t just idiosyncratic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re going to want to see, you know, continued progress with housing services inflation; you’re going to want to see inflation behaving in a way that builds confidence that we are really making progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what it’s going to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, I mean, is, is that better than our expectations?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we expect to see that, it’s just a question of when.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Scott.

speaker: SCOTT HORSLEY
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: SCOTT HORSLEY
sentence: Scott Horsley from NPR.

speaker: SCOTT HORSLEY
sentence: In your five-year review, you said the, the 2 percent inflation target won’t be on the table.

speaker: SCOTT HORSLEY
sentence: Can you talk a little about why?

speaker: SCOTT HORSLEY
sentence: Is that because you think that’s the right target, or is it because you don’t want to move the goalpost midgame, or what’s, what’s behind that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think to—I think that goal has served us well over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also the sort of global standard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that if, if a central bank wanted to look at changing that, you wouldn’t do it at a time when you’re not meeting it anyway.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would not look at changing it anyway, but I certainly wouldn’t look at, at it at a time when you’re not—when you’re not meeting it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, there’s just no interest at all in changing it, if, if I’m being at all unclear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not—we’re not going to change the inflation goal any time soon.

speaker: SCOTT HORSLEY
sentence: And, and five years ago, if I can paraphrase what you all decided, it was you’re going to not raise interest rates preemptively to, to head off inflation until you see sort of the whites of the eyes of inflation, because the solid labor market was so beneficial.

speaker: SCOTT HORSLEY
sentence: Have the last few years changed your thinking about that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what we really said was that we wouldn’t—we wouldn’t look at a—at a strong labor market and raise rates unless we saw some evidence of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the thought was that we’d seen really low levels of inflation—sorry, of unemployment—with no sign of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So why would you preemptively want to—want to put people out of work in the absence of, of any kind of—any evidence that suggested that, that this was not a sustainable level?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was a way of, of acknowledging how much humility we have about, about the starred variables, especially u*, the natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, that was a—that, that was an insight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll, we’ll discuss that again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’ll be one of the many things that we discuss.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I don’t think that insight is wrong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We didn’t—you know, we, we—what we said was that, you know, in—at times when inflation persistently undershot 2 percent, we, we would likely allow inflation to run moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That was—turned out not to be relevant to what actually happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There was nothing moderate about the overshoot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was—it was an exogenous event.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was the pandemic, and it happened, and, you know, our framework permitted us to act quite vigorously, and we did once we decided that that’s what we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our framework had really nothing to do with the decision to—we, we looked at the inflation as, as transitory, and—right up to the point where the data turned against that, and when the data turned against that in late ’21, we changed our, our view, and we raised rates a lot, and here we are at 4.1 percent unemployment and inflation way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the framework was, was more irrelevant than anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The, the, that part of it—that part of it was irrelevant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The rest of the framework worked just fine as, as we used it, as it supported what we did to bring inflation down.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Go to Mark for the last question.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: Hello, Chairman Powell.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: Mark Hamrick with Bankrate.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: As you know, in the annual report from the Financial Stability Oversight Council, among the risks outlined is cryptocurrency.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: Could you talk about those risks now?

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: And regarding individuals and households, perhaps distinct from the concern about the financial system, do you worry that speculation in this unregulated asset class could hurt their financial well-being, or do you think it has a place in a household’s portfolio?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, so our, our role with Bitcoin, really, is to look at—with crypto, really, is to look at the banks, and, and, you know, we, we think it’s—you know, banks are perfectly able to serve crypto customers, as long as they understand and can manage the risks and its safe, safe and soundness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Many of our—a good number of our banks that we regulate and supervise do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the threshold has been a little higher for banks engaging in crypto activities, and that’s because they’re so new, and, you know, we don’t want to make the mistake you’re—if you—if you’re making a choice to conduct that activity inside a bank which is inside the federal safety net, with deposit insurance, then you want to be pretty sure that, that it’s a safe and sound activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we’re, we’re not against innovation, and we certainly don’t want to, to take actions that would cause banks to, you know, to terminate customers who are perfectly legal just because of, of excess risk aversion maybe related to regulation and supervision, so.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: And with respect to households and their inclusion in that asset class?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, you know, that’s, that’s kind of a—it’s not really our, our bailiwick.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You want people to be knowledgeable about the financial engagements that they have, and that’s why we have, you know, the securities law, laws that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s why, you know, if you read a mutual fund prospectus or individual stock prospectus, you, you want households to have the chance to understand the risk that they’re taking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I, I do think it would be helpful if there were a greater regulatory apparatus around crypto, and I think that, that’s something Congress was working on quite a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve actually spent a lot of time, you know, with members of Congress working together with them on, on various things, and I, I think that would be a very constructive thing for, for Congress to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.
